title: The Last Name on the Register
excerpt: A night archivist finds names being used after death and one living woman marked for midnight. She has until dawn to expose the fraud.

sections.title: Names for the Night
paragraphs: In the city of Bellwether, a vampire could drink only from a willing person whose name appeared on the night's register. The rule had ended a century of hunting. It had also made the archive the most dangerous building in town.

Iris Venn worked there after dark, checking signatures against consent cards and stamping permits in blue ink. She had never seen a donor attacked in the streets, which was the promise the system made. She had seen people sell a pint of blood for rent, then return before their bodies recovered, which was the cost no official poster mentioned. Her job was to keep the names honest. She had believed, until Tuesday, that she did.

Tuesday's first mistake was a woman named Miriam Bell. Miriam's card was renewed at six o'clock. At seven, the hospital sent notice that she had died the previous winter. Someone had used her signature again. Iris pulled the past month's registers. Miriam had donated six times since her death, each permit assigned to a different vampire and signed with the same careful loop on the final letter. The fraud was clumsy enough to have been noticed by anyone who looked, yet no one had.

The second mistake had her own handwriting on it. The renewal stamp belonged to her desk. She checked the clock and remembered leaving at five to take soup to her brother, Niko. At six, someone had entered the archive with her key or an exact copy. The watchman's log showed no visitor. Iris photographed the card and slipped it back before the chief registrar arrived.

A third name appeared in the stack: Leona Hart. Alive, thirty-two, consent withdrawn three months earlier. Her cancellation had been crossed out with blue ink and replaced by a permit for midnight. The assigned recipient was listed as V. Sable, the chief registrar's private account.

Iris found Leona's address in the old correspondence file and went out beneath the rain. She did not know whether the card meant a feeding, an assault, or some accounting trick. She knew midnight was four hours away. On the tram she called Niko, who worked as a courier for the night hospital. He offered to meet her. She told him to stay at work. He asked whether she was in trouble. She said she was finding out.

Leona lived above a tailor's shop. When Iris knocked, a voice behind the door said, 'I withdrew consent. I have the letter.' Iris showed her archive badge through the glass. Leona opened the door a fraction. She was packing a suitcase, the room scattered with folded clothes and torn envelopes. Someone had visited the previous night, asking her to renew her donation. When she refused, he had said the register already proved she had agreed.
'His name?' Iris asked.
'I didn't ask. He knew mine.' Leona's gaze fell on the photograph on Iris's phone. 'That's not my signature.'

Iris zoomed in. The same loop finished Miriam's name and Leona's. Whoever forged them had written both with one hand. A permit alone could not compel a donor to submit; the law required a witness at the clinic. But a forged permit could make a disappearance appear consensual afterward. Iris helped Leona lock the shop and brought her to Niko at the hospital, where the night staff knew how to keep an unwanted visitor outside.
At the hospital entrance, Leona touched Iris's sleeve. 'Why are you helping me?'
'Because the register says you asked for something you didn't.'
'People say that all the time.'
Iris thought of the cards she had stamped without looking closely. 'Then I should have listened sooner.'

sections.title: The Archive Under the Archive
paragraphs: Niko knew a doctor who handled blood bags too old for patients but still suitable for vampires. The bags were supposed to go to the city supply office. For weeks, fewer had been collected than the hospital recorded. The shortage had pushed more vampires toward direct donors, raising the price of every permit. If someone sold stolen hospital blood through the register, dead donors would be ideal names: nobody would come back to complain.

Iris returned to the archive with Niko, who insisted on carrying a flashlight and a small first-aid kit. The watchman had gone for coffee. They entered through the delivery door and searched the basement accounts. Payments to V. Sable came from a company called Bellwether Night Relief. The company owned three refrigerated vans and a warehouse by the canal. Its directors were hidden behind a trust signed by the chief registrar, Vera Sable.

Niko found another folder with the recent donor cards. Dozens of names belonged to people reported dead. Several belonged to people who were still alive but had withdrawn consent. Iris's initials appeared on every renewal, traced from her old stamps. She felt a burst of absurd relief that the forger had copied the angle of her pen badly. Then she understood what the file was for: if anyone investigated, the trail would lead to her desk.

A voice came from the stairs. Vera Sable stood there in a dark coat, without guards. She was a vampire older than the city charter and had spent the past twenty years telling schoolchildren why consent mattered. She looked tired rather than frightened.
'I hoped you'd find the warehouse first,' Vera said. 'Then you might understand the arithmetic.'
Iris held up Miriam's card. 'A dead woman cannot consent.'
'No one drank from Miriam. That name covered a bag the hospital would have thrown away.'
'Leona is alive.'

Vera looked at the card and for the first time seemed uncertain. She said she had authorized only expired blood under dead donors' names, to keep the supply open while the Council debated a new ration. She had not signed Leona's permit. Her assistant, Dorian Pell, managed the trucks. He had argued that direct donations would be more profitable and easier to move. Vera had refused. Now he was using the same false ledger for something worse.

Niko asked why Vera had hidden the shortage in the first place. She answered that the Council would close the archive if it learned she had broken the charter. Iris said that might be exactly what they should do. Vera did not argue. She handed over a brass key to the canal warehouse and told them the vans left at eleven-thirty. It was ten-fifteen.
'Come with us,' Iris said.
Vera stared at the names in the folder. 'If I go, they'll protect him by saying I planned it all.'
'You did plan part of it.'
A long silence followed. Vera took the folder from Iris and walked upstairs with them.

sections.title: The Woman Who First Signed
paragraphs: Before they went to the warehouse, Iris made Niko stop at the apartment of their aunt Elian. She was not a vampire and had never donated, but she had worked as a court translator during the charter hearings. She remembered why the register had been written in such rigid language. In the years before it, families had hidden their children from night patrols, and vampires had hidden from mobs in cellars. The compromise did not make everyone friends. It made each person's refusal visible in a place the city had to respect.

Elian read Leona's false card under a lamp. She found a clause on the reverse that Iris had never noticed: consent could be withdrawn before the appointed hour, even after a permit was issued. The clause was printed in small type because the Council had wanted permits to appear final to buyers. Elian had argued against that choice at the hearing and lost. She was angry to see how useful the small type had become to men like Dorian.
'If Leona signs a new withdrawal and we file it in front of witnesses,' she said, 'no one can claim the midnight permit protects them.'
Leona took the pen. Her hand shook. She stopped and put it down. 'I'm tired of signing things because someone else has made me afraid.'
'You don't have to,' Iris said.

'I want the right to be on record. I just want you to hear what I'm saying first.' Leona looked at each of them. 'I never consented. I never changed my mind. If anything happens to me, it is a crime. I need those words written down.'

Iris wrote them on a clean sheet. Elian and Niko witnessed it. Leona signed beneath her own statement, not beneath a form someone had prepared for her. Elian pressed an old court stamp into the page and gave Leona a copy. The small act took ten minutes. It did not make the warehouse safe, but it kept Dorian from claiming the most important part of his story had been agreed to.
On the way downstairs, Elian caught Iris's arm. 'You think the archive failed because one registrar was greedy. It failed because no one could see inside it. When this is over, remember that.'

Iris did. She could still smell the archive's dust on her coat. She had loved the quiet there and the neatness of closed drawers. Now she wondered how many people had stood outside its door and been told their own records were too private for them to inspect.

sections.title: A City That Looked Away
paragraphs: The hospital's records showed the shortage began after a heat wave damaged the western cold store. The Council had delayed repairs, preferring to praise a new monument in the central square. Vera had covered the gap with expired bags and fraudulent names. Dorian had discovered the method and found a darker market for it. Each person had made the next deception easier.

Niko drove the clinic van to the canal. Leona sat beside Iris with a paper cup of tea she never drank. She had refused to hide at the hospital once she learned her name was still on the midnight permit. 'If they bring someone in my place, I need to know,' she said. Iris did not try to stop her. She had spent too long deciding what other people ought to know about their own names.

At the warehouse gate they found a guard wearing an archive badge. He recognized Vera and opened the chain. Inside, five refrigerators hummed beneath exposed pipes. Two were filled with labeled hospital bags. The third was empty. The fourth held a chair, restraints, and a tray of consent forms already signed. The fifth held a ledger of addresses. Leona found her own apartment listed beside three others. She folded the page into her coat without asking permission.

Dorian entered from the loading bay carrying a silver case. He was human, with neat hair and a courteous voice. Vera demanded to know where the donors were. He said they were safe and would remain so if she let the van leave. He had paid them for a private service, he claimed. The forms were evidence. Leona pointed to the copy of her signature and asked when she had been paid. Dorian looked at her, then at Iris, and understood the forged card had been found early.

He drew a small pistol. Niko moved between him and Leona. Vera crossed the room faster than anyone could follow. She caught Dorian's wrist before he fired, but he struck a switch on the wall with his free hand. The warehouse lights died. The refrigerators went silent. In the dark, Iris heard a door slam and a van engine start.
Vera held Dorian against the floor. He laughed once. 'You think I used your trucks without making arrangements? The Council treasurer owns the second van.'
Iris followed the engine sound through the loading bay. The van was already turning toward the bridge. She saw a face at its rear window, then a palm pressed to the glass. Someone was inside.

Niko came running with the keys to the clinic van. He could not drive and watch the road behind them, so Iris took the passenger seat and called the night watch. The dispatcher wanted a permit number before sending anyone. Iris gave him the warehouse address, the van plate, and the name of the person she had seen through the window: a young man on the register named Pavel Reed. His card had been renewed after his death too. According to the official file he had been buried in March.
The dispatcher paused. 'If he's dead, who is in the van?'
'Find out with us,' Iris said.

sections.title: A Ledger of Small Favors
paragraphs: At the warehouse, while Vera held Dorian and Iris chased the van, Leona searched the office upstairs. She found envelopes of cash, each marked with a date and the initials of a different Council member. Beneath them lay receipts for food, rent, and hospital bills paid for people whose names had been entered as dead. Dorian had bought silence in two ways: by bribing officials who could erase files and by making frightened witnesses depend on him to survive.

Leona recognized one address. It belonged to Pavel's mother. She had taken money after being told her son was alive but in danger. Every month a courier brought an envelope and a warning not to call the police. Leona folded the receipt into her pocket. She did not know whether Pavel's mother had believed the warning or the money. She knew the choice had been made under a threat.

Vera read the receipts without speaking. For years she had presented the register as proof that her city was civilized. Her own illegal supply scheme had made Dorian's first false entries look ordinary. When Leona asked why she had not audited him, Vera said she had been afraid of what a full audit would reveal about her. The answer was plain, and Leona hated it more than a clever excuse.

She made Vera call the magistrate before anyone left the warehouse. Vera gave her name, her location, and the nature of the fraud. Then Leona asked the dispatcher to repeat it back so there would be a record outside Vera's control. She photographed the frozen room and its restraints, the listed addresses, and the receipts. The night watch arrived after Iris and Niko had driven off. By then Leona had three copies of the evidence: one on her phone, one sent to Elian, and one handed to a guard whose body camera was running.

The magistrate asked whether Leona was a witness or a complainant. 'Both,' she said. She wanted the city to know that a living person had seen the forged card before midnight. She wanted any future inquiry to begin with that fact, not with the tidy explanation the Council would write after sunrise.

sections.title: The Bridge at Midnight
paragraphs: The canal bridge rose for freight boats at midnight. If the van crossed before it lifted, it could reach the private airfield beyond the city. Niko drove hard through rain slick streets. Leona stayed at the warehouse with Vera, photographing every form and locking the doors before the Council could remove the files. Iris saw the van's tail lights at the bridge approach, then a red signal as the barrier began to fall.

The van accelerated. Niko slowed, knowing they would not clear it safely. Iris shouted for him to stop. The van clipped the barrier and spun. Its rear wheel hit the curb. A moment later it stood still, engine whining, rear doors jammed against a post. Two men escaped from the cab. One ran toward the rail yard; the other slipped on the wet pavement and was caught by the watch officers arriving from the opposite side.

Iris went to the rear doors. A person inside was kicking them from within. Niko found the emergency latch, but it had been wired shut. He cut the wire with a pair of medical shears. Pavel Reed fell forward, alive and shaking. His hair had been cut short since the photograph in the archive. He said he had reported the stolen bags to the hospital in March. Two days later a death certificate appeared in his name. He had been kept in a locked room while Dorian used that certificate to obtain permits. He did not know why they were moving him tonight. His testimony would make the entire fraud impossible to dismiss as an accounting error.

Behind him sat two other people, both alive, both listed as dead. The van carried medical coolers and travel documents with new names. Dorian's operation had been moving witnesses out of the city under false identities, telling them the Council would kill them if they stayed. Perhaps some had chosen to go. Pavel said he had not.

At the hospital, Iris stayed while the three gave statements. She called the families named in their files. One father did not believe her until he heard his son's voice. Iris listened to their reunion over a poor phone connection and thought of every time she had treated a signature as the whole of a person.

Vera arrived near dawn with the warehouse records. She had gone first to the night magistrate and turned herself in. Dorian's lawyers would say she had forged the cards and invented the kidnapping to protect her own trade. Vera had brought the original payment ledger and the key to her private account. 'I can prove where my part ends,' she said. 'I won't pretend it never began.'

The treasurer was arrested before sunrise. The Council announced an inquiry. Their statement mentioned public confidence more than the people whose names had been stolen. Leona read it once and set it aside.

sections.title: The Hearing in Daylight
paragraphs: The inquiry began in daylight, which meant several vampire witnesses testified through shaded glass. Council lawyers argued that the old register had prevented far more violence than it had allowed. Iris agreed. Then she placed Miriam Bell's six renewed permits on the table and asked which of them the Council would have caught if she had stayed silent. No one answered.

Pavel testified next. He described the room where he had been held, the false death certificate, and the moment he saw his own name on a permit. His father sat in the back row. When Pavel struggled to continue, the magistrate offered a break. Pavel asked instead to finish while he still had the courage. He said he had trusted the archive more than the police because its signatures were supposed to matter. Seeing his forged signature had been worse than seeing the locked door: the door told him he was trapped; the paper told the city he had chosen it.

Leona brought her withdrawal, signed with Elian and Niko as witnesses. The Council's lawyer suggested that she had been confused by the process. She asked him to read the sentence she had written in her own words. He did, slowly. By the time he reached the end, the room had gone still.

Vera did not ask to be excused because Dorian had exploited her scheme. She explained the shortage, the expired bags, and the false renewals. She named the meetings at which the Council delayed repairs to the cold store. The treasurer objected, saying those meetings had been routine budget debates. Iris produced the minutes, which included the exact cost of replacing the cooling units beside a vote to postpone it. The choice had been made in full view. Only its consequences had been hidden.

The hearing lasted four days. By the end, the magistrate ordered the archive's records opened to the people named in them and referred the criminal charges to trial. The Council announced reforms quickly, as councils do when their records are on a public table. Iris and Leona read the proposal together. It gave donors a new way to sign, but no easy way to check whether old permissions remained active. They returned it with that omission marked in red. The city could keep its charter. It had to let the people inside it read the terms.

sections.title: The Names That Came Back
paragraphs: The court could punish Dorian, but it could not tell every family what had happened to the person they mourned. Iris volunteered to help the hospital verify the death certificates. She expected to find a list of numbers. She found birthdays, street addresses, and notes in margins: loved spicy soup, afraid of stairs, called every Sunday. Dorian's forged papers had been designed to erase those details. Iris put them back into the inquiry files so that each record held more than a date of disappearance.

One woman named Alina had been reported dead while working on a ship beyond the harbor. She returned to find her apartment rented to strangers and her daughter living with an uncle who had told her that Alina had abandoned her. The daughter was fourteen. She did not run into Alina's arms when they met at the hospital. She asked why her mother had not called. Alina showed her the letters she had written and never managed to deliver. They sat together for an hour, reading without touching. Iris had wanted a reunion that proved all could be repaired. She left them space for the harder work that actually lay ahead.

Another name belonged to a vampire, a musician called Tomas who had challenged Vera's supply figures. Dorian had removed him from the register entirely, marking him as having left the city. Tomas had hidden with friends after two men attacked him outside his rehearsal room. His testimony mattered because the fraud had harmed vampires too. They depended on the system for lawful access to blood and for the public proof that they could live without hunting. A corrupt register made every consent doubtful and every old fear easier to revive.

At an open meeting, a donor asked whether the new system would publish everyone's address. Iris said no. Transparency of a permit did not require exposing a home. They spent two evenings working out a simple distinction: the person named could inspect every record about themselves; the public could see totals and rules; investigators could see private details only with a court order. Leona insisted on a plain-language explanation beside each form. Tomas wanted a way to challenge a shortage report before a rumor became a panic. Pavel asked for a visible correction process so a false death could never remain in one database after being fixed in another.

They argued. Some left and came back. Iris found that a table crowded with complaints was more honest than the silent room of drawers she had loved. She began to understand Elian's warning: a system could be carefully designed and still become cruel if the people it governed were treated as obstacles to its neatness.

One evening Niko came in carrying soup for everyone. He had been the one to drive toward the bridge, but afterward people thanked Iris first. She told the room what he had done. Niko shook his head, embarrassed, and gave the largest bowl to Pavel. Later he admitted he had been afraid she would lose her job and blame herself for every card she had stamped. Iris said she had lost the job. She also had the chance to make a better one. Niko said those were not the same thing. She agreed, and they sat together while the others kept arguing about ink colors and access codes.

sections.title: The Cost of the Cold Store
paragraphs: The new supply figures made a different problem visible. Several vampires had been living on emergency rations while the Council delayed repairs. One of them, an elderly woman named Ruth, came to the open meeting with a cracked thermos and a list of neighbors who had shared their portions. She was angry with Vera for hiding the shortage. She was also angry with the people who assumed vampires would become violent if they were told the truth. 'I know how to be hungry without hurting someone,' she said. 'I cannot solve a shortage I am forbidden to know exists.'

The city repaired the western cold store. During the work, Niko helped audit the hospital transfers. Iris watched him reconcile each bag against a patient record, its expiration date, and the chain of custody. The process was slower than Vera's secret ledger. It was also legible to a nurse who had never met the chief registrar. Niko found two missing shipments that had been blamed on the heat wave but had left the hospital after the cooling system was fixed. They were traced to a Council contractor who had sold them to Dorian. The contractor's name had appeared in the inquiry once and almost vanished beneath the larger charges.

Leona insisted the final report include that trail. She had learned how quickly a case could be reduced to one bad man when many people had opened doors for him. She also insisted on a notice to every person who had withdrawn consent in the previous two years. The notice would say whether the withdrawal had been honored, not merely that the city was confident in its new process. Some recipients called to say they had never felt unsafe. Others called with questions nobody could answer yet. Iris stayed on the phone until each caller had a name to contact again.

One caller was Miriam Bell's daughter. She knew her mother could not have donated after death, but seeing six official records under her name felt like losing her again. Iris apologized for stamping them. The daughter said an apology mattered, but she wanted the false entries preserved with corrections attached. Erasing them would make it harder to prove what had happened. Iris changed the archive procedure that afternoon: every corrected card kept its original image beside the explanation. The register would remember its own mistakes.

Niko put the corrected supply sheet on the hospital noticeboard before his shift ended. A young vampire stopped to read it, then asked whether the next week's figures would appear there too. Niko said they would. It was a small promise, visible enough that anyone could remind him if he forgot.

sections.title: The Night Clerk's Desk
paragraphs: On her last day in the old archive, Iris cleared her desk while workers removed the locked drawers. She found a folder of requests from donors who had asked to see their records. Most had been denied under a privacy rule written to protect them from public curiosity. The letters had never reached Vera. They sat in a clerk's tray, answered with a form paragraph that Iris herself had stamped. One came from Leona, dated weeks before the false midnight permit. She had asked whether her withdrawal was visible to every clinic. Iris had sent the standard reply: your records are secure.
She took the folder to Leona. Leona read her own letter and did not hide her anger. 'If someone had answered the question,' she said, 'I would have known the cancellation never reached the clinic.'

Iris agreed. She did not explain that she had been overworked or that the rule had been older than her job. Those things were true and did not change the answer Leona had needed. Together they sorted the requests by date. Some writers had moved away. Two had died. Iris called the living people she could find and explained the new inspection process. Several thanked her; one hung up. She wrote down each response so the new office would not treat silence as satisfaction.

The last letter was from Ruth, the elderly vampire who had spoken at the supply meeting. She had asked to see how many donated bags had expired before distribution, afraid that scarcity was being made worse by waste. The archive had rejected her because she was not a donor. Iris called Ruth and invited her to review the public supply figures. Ruth arrived with a pencil and found a transcription error in ten minutes. She stayed for two hours to help correct it.

The room with windows was not quiet like Iris's old office. People asked questions while she worked. She answered some and admitted when she did not know the others. By closing, her desk was messy with notes. Every person who came in had been able to see the record that concerned them. Iris left the blinds open when she went home.

sections.title: The Blank Page
paragraphs: The archive was closed for six weeks. Iris lost her job during the investigation and spent the first three days sleeping at odd hours, her body unused to daylight. Then Leona asked her to help build a way for donors to see every use of their names. They met in the tailor's shop with Niko, Pavel, two clinic workers, and anyone else who wanted a seat. The first rule they wrote was simple: no one should need an archivist's favor to learn whether their consent had been recorded or withdrawn.

The new register opened in a room with windows. Every donor received a copy of each permit and a code they could use to cancel it. The city posted the supply figures every week. Expired hospital blood was governed by a separate process, named honestly on the label. Vampires who had relied on it argued over the new ration. Some were frightened. Some were furious. Iris understood both without agreeing that fear excused forgery.

Vera testified in court. She lost her office and accepted a sentence that kept her from handling blood records again. Dorian and the treasurer faced charges for kidnapping and falsifying deaths. The outcome did not repair the months stolen from Pavel or the terror Leona had felt when her own door became unsafe. No system could reverse that. But the people affected could finally testify as themselves.

One evening Leona brought Iris a small card from the tailor's shop. On it she had sewn a line of red thread through the words I CHOOSE. Iris laughed at the handmade formality, then kept the card in her wallet. She had spent years believing the archive's strength was its old stone walls and guarded drawers. What saved the people on its lists had been the opposite: a door they could open, a page they could inspect, a voice allowed to say no.
At closing time Iris turned to the final sheet of the new register. It was blank except for the date. She left it that way until the first person came to write a name by choice.
